blocks.text: But the two Arabic versions have here شاهين [shāhīn] sahin, which Giggeius ineptly renders swan or porphyrio, since the sahin is a bird of prey and one of the τῶν γαμψωνύχων [tōn gampsōnychōn]. Of it Alkazuinius says: طير معروف من جوارح [col. 288] الطير عدو الحمام اذا راه الحمام يعتريه ما يعتري الشاه من الذيب والغار من الهر والحمام اسرع طيرانا منه الا انه اذا راه يضعف عن الطيران خوفا واذا راته السلحفاه ويعطيه ظهرها فلا يعمل منقار الشاهين فيها فيحملها الشاهين ويصعد بها نحو السما ويرميها علي حجر صلد لتنكسرت فياكلها واذا مرض الشاهين اكل الدراريج يزول مرضه [ṭayr maʿrūf min jawāriḥ al-ṭayr ʿadūw al-ḥamām idhā raʾāhu al-ḥamām yaʿtarīhi mā yaʿtarī al-shāh min al-dhīb wa-al-ghār min al-hirr wa-al-ḥamām asraʿ ṭayarānan minhu illā annahu idhā raʾāhu yaḍʿuf ʿan al-ṭayarān khawfan wa-idhā raʾathu al-sulaḥfāh wa-yuʿṭīhi ẓahrahā fa-lā yaʿmal minqār al-shāhīn fīhā fa-yaḥmiluhā al-shāhīn wa-yaṣʿad bihā naḥw al-samā wa-yarmīhā ʿalā ḥajar ṣald li-tankasirat fa-yaʾkuluhā wa-idhā mariḍa al-shāhīn akala al-darārīj yazūl maraḍuhu] “A well-known bird of the raptorial kind. It is a bird hostile to doves. When doves see the sahin, the same thing happens to them as to a sheep [III, 34] at the sight of a wolf, and to a mouse at the sight of a cat. For although the dove surpasses it in flight, yet when it sees it, it grows weak with fear. The tortoise turns its back to it, against which the beak of the sahin can do nothing; but the sahin seizes it, lifts it up to the heavens and throws it down onto a hard stone, so as to eat it once broken. When the sahin is sick, it is cured by eating cantharides.” And Damir, after explaining that in the plural one says شيواهين [shīwāhīn] saivvahin and شياهين [shiyāhīn] sajahin, that the word is in use among the Arabs although it is foreign, and that there are three kinds of it, 1. the sahin properly so called; 2. قطامي [quṭāmī] kotami, that is, greedy for flesh; 3. انيقي [anīqī] aniki, or, as another copy has it, اسقي [asqī] aski, describes the first kind thus: الشاهين في الحقيقه من جنس الصقر الا انه ابرد وايبس منه مزاجا ولاجل ذلك تكون حركته من العلو الي اسفل شديدة ولهذا ينقض علي صيده انقضاضا من غير تحويم وعنده جبن وفتور وهو مع ذلك شديد الضراوة علي الصيد ولاجل ذلك ربما ضرب بنفسه الارض ومات وعظامه صلب من عظام ساير الجوارح وبعضهم يقول الشاهين كاسمه يعني الميزان لانه لا يحتمل ادني حال من [col. 289] الشبع ولا ادني حال من الجوع المحمود من صفاته ان يكون عظيم الهامة واسع العينين رحب الصدر ممتلي الزور عريض الوسط غليظ ^{a)} الفخذين قصير الساعدين ^{b)} قليل الريش رقيق الذنب اذا صلب عليه جناحيه لم يفضل منه شي واذا كان كذلك صاد الكركي وغيره [al-shāhīn fī al-ḥaqīqa min jins al-ṣaqr illā annahu abrad wa-aybas minhu mizājan wa-li-ajl dhālika takūn ḥarakatuhu min al-ʿuluw ilā asfal shadīda wa-li-hādhā yanqaḍḍ ʿalā ṣaydihi inqiḍāḍan min ghayr taḥwīm wa-ʿindahu jubn wa-futūr wa-huwa maʿa dhālika shadīd al-ḍarāwa ʿalā al-ṣayd wa-li-ajl dhālika rubbamā ḍaraba bi-nafsihi al-arḍ wa-māta wa-ʿiẓāmuhu ṣulb min ʿiẓām sāyir al-jawāriḥ wa-baʿḍuhum yaqūl al-shāhīn ka-smihi yaʿnī al-mīzān li-annahu lā yaḥtamil adnā ḥāl min al-shibaʿ wa-lā adnā ḥāl min al-jūʿ al-maḥmūd min ṣifātihi an yakūn ʿaẓīm al-hāma wāsiʿ al-ʿaynayn raḥb al-ṣadr mumtaliʾ al-zawr ʿarīḍ al-wasaṭ ghalīẓ al-fakhdhayn qaṣīr al-sāʿidayn qalīl al-rīsh raqīq al-dhanab idhā ṣaluba ʿalayhi janāḥayhi lam yafḍul minhu shayʾ wa-idhā kāna ka-dhālika ṣāda al-kurkī wa-ghayrahu] “The true sahin is of the saker kind, except that it is of a colder and drier temperament, and hence its movement is most powerful from above downwards. That is why it descends upon its prey without any circling. And although it is sluggish and slack by nature, it is carried to the hunt with such force that it sometimes hurls itself headlong to the ground and dies. Yet it has harder bones than any other bird of prey. Some assert that the name sahin means balance, because this bird cannot bear the slightest hunger nor the slightest satiety. The most highly prized of this kind is the one with a large head, wide eyes, a broad chest, a full upper breast, a broad middle, thick thighs, short arms (var. legs), few feathers and a slender tail. If along with these marks it has strong wings, nothing will be more excellent, and it will hunt cranes and other birds of that sort.” He goes on to say that this kind of hawking [III, 35] first originated with Constantine, emperor of the Romans, who had الشواهين [al-shawāhīn] sahins trained to fly above his head and to give him shade, so that he would not be scorched by the heat of the sun. I also have in my possession a French book entitled Conference des fauconniers, that is, Conference of Falconers. In it, in the tenth conference, the sahins are described thus: “The sahins are falcons of high rank, which have a head flat on top and plumage edged with white and also evenly marked with russet. Hence it seems that nature has placed on their head a garland or crown, as a mark of their excellence. In short, these are the falcons which were formerly called peregrines, or Tartar falcons, although this was improperly said” ^{(4)}. And the most distinguished Thuanus, after saying that it is called Peregrine because its origins are uncertain, describes it thus in book 1 of On Falconry, page 14:

— — a large head, a lofty neck, a flattened crown: from here a white line runs crosswise along each temple and meets, and crowns the broad top, and, with the neck bent back, at length branches off into several strands, girding the neck with an artful chain. The body is not so huge; but it has a long thigh and slender wings, short legs, and a short tail guides its swift efforts against the opposing air.
See the rest there, and you will find that it agrees with the description of the Arabs.
